blocks.content: Albrecht Dürer, 1514. Engraving, about 24 × 19 cm. Impressions are held by many museums.

A winged figure sits among the instruments of every exact art: compass, scale, plane, saw, hourglass. She is holding the compass and not using it. Nothing in the picture is broken. Everything needed for work is within reach, and no work is being done.

The best known reading, Erwin Panofsky’s, takes the print as a portrait of the mind that can measure everything and still cannot reach what it wants to know. Other scholars disagree, and Dürer left no explanation.
Look at it large. Give it ten minutes before reading anything else about it.
The square of numbers on the wall: every row, column and diagonal adds up to 34. The two middle cells of the bottom row read 15 and 14, the year.
The large stone solid has never been conclusively explained. It is usually described as a cube stretched and then cut at two corners.
On the ground: a plane, a saw, a ruler, nails. Carpenter’s tools, scattered rather than put away.
The title is carried by a bat-like creature. Nobody knows what the “I” stands for.
